title: Dividends and borrow, read off the options
lede: Page 03 built parity at one expiry, and page 17 will use it to fix the forward before reading implied vols. This page lines the forwards up across expiries. The result is a term structure of carry, and three things follow from it: where the dividends sit, what the stock costs to borrow at each horizon, and who gains or loses when a dividend changes.

chapters.title: Each expiry quotes one number, and the numbers make a curve
chapters.dek: Take call-minus-put at every expiry, turn each into a forward, and ask how much each forward gives up against simply holding the stock on borrowed money.

figures.title: Carry to each expiry, per year
figures.caption: A sawtooth that dies away. Each tooth is a dividend arriving; the level it settles to is the dividend yield plus the borrow.

checks.q: The two-month expiry implies 4.6% carry and the one-year implies 3.4%. The stock pays a quarterly dividend. What is the likeliest reading?
checks.right: One dividend falls inside two months, and a lump over a short time annualizes high
checks.why: A dividend in a short window. Before blaming borrow, subtract the dividends you know about. What is left is the borrow curve, and on this stock it is flat at 1%. The first answer is what the same picture would mean on a stock that pays nothing.

chapters.text: A $100 stock pays 60 cents a quarter, costs 1% a year to borrow, and money is at 4.5%. The red dots are the eight listed expiries. For each one the figure takes the forward that parity implies and annualizes its shortfall against 100 grown at 4.5%. The dashed line is the same stock with the dividend removed. Carry to each expiry, per year The stock A sawtooth that dies away. Each tooth is a dividend arriving; the level it settles to is the dividend yield plus the borrow. The thirty-day expiry reads 1.00%, because no dividend falls inside it and all it sees is borrow. The sixty-day reads 4.64%: one 60-cent dividend spread over two months is a large annual rate. By a year the curve has settled at 3.38%, close to the 2.4% yield plus the 1% fee. So a single expiry's carry is hard to read by itself. A front-month number of 4.6% on this stock is not expensive borrow; it is a dividend divided by a short time, the same arithmetic that makes event vol look enormous on page 03. [equation: carry(T) = r − ln( F(T) / S ) / T] Reads as: the interest rate, minus the rate at which the forward actually grows from spot. Whatever is missing went to the people who hold the shares: dividends to the owner, fees to the lender. Try this Make the stock hard to borrow now, easing later. Predict which end of the curve rises most. The front rises most: 10.5% to thirty days against 5.6% to two years. A borrow squeeze the market expects to pass shows up as an inverted carry curve, and the long-dated options barely notice. That is the difference between a name that is hard to borrow this month and one that is structurally hard to borrow, and it is visible before you ask a stock-loan desk anything.

chapters.title: Between two expiries there is exactly one unknown
chapters.dek: The carry from one expiry to the next is what a jelly roll trades. Fix the borrow and it tells you the dividend; fix the dividend and it tells you the borrow.

figures.title: Dividend implied by each pair of expiries
figures.caption: Each bar is as tall as the dividends inside its interval: 60 cents where there is one ex-date, nothing where there is none, $1.20 where there are two. The lower panel prices one roll across strikes. It is a straight line: its slope is interest on the strike, about a cent per dollar of strike over these three months, and the gap below the grey line is the dividend and borrow. Strike changes the interest you lend at, never the dividend you are betting on.

figures.title: Trade the roll into the board meeting
figures.caption: In the first round the market prices an 18% chance that a quiet board suspends a $0.80 dividend, so the roll implies $0.658; the board pays the $0.80 and a bought roll makes $710. Over 2,000 rounds, buying every roll loses about $35 a round and selling every one makes about the same: the market's number is close to fair on average. Trading only where your chance of a cut differs from the market's averages $331 a round. The roll pays for being right about the dividend and for nothing else.

checks.q: A company's declared dividend is $0.60. The interval containing the next ex-date implies $0.45, using your stock-loan desk's borrow quote. Which is the weakest conclusion?
checks.right: The options are mispriced and the roll is free money
checks.why: Free money is the weakest. The other three are each a real explanation and each can be checked: the company's payout history, a second borrow quote, the ex-date calendar. Until those are ruled out the roll is a bet on a dividend, with the people who know the company best on the other side.

chapters.text: The figure takes each pair of neighboring expiries and asks what cash dividend the gap between their forwards implies, given a borrow fee you supply. The dotted lines are the dates the company is expected to go ex. Then it lets the market disagree with the company about the fourth one. Dividend implied by each pair of expiries The same roll (273 → 365 days) priced at every strike The market, and your assumption Each bar is as tall as the dividends inside its interval: 60 cents where there is one ex-date, nothing where there is none, $1.20 where there are two. The lower panel prices one roll across strikes. It is a straight line: its slope is interest on the strike, about a cent per dollar of strike over these three months, and the gap below the grey line is the dividend and borrow. Strike changes the interest you lend at, never the dividend you are betting on. Try this The market starts pricing the fourth dividend at half. Predict which bar moves, and whether any other does. Only the bar from 273 to 365 days moves, from 60 cents to 30. Every other interval is untouched, because a forward-to-forward comparison sees only what happens between its two dates. In prices: the jelly roll at the 100 strike across that interval goes from $0.27 to $0.56. Somebody long the far synthetic and short the near one has made 29 cents a share on a dividend that has not been announced. The second button is the caution. Leave the dividend alone and read the same chain assuming 3% borrow when the market is using 1%, and every bar shrinks: the interval from 91 to 182 days reads 10 cents instead of 60, and the one with no dividend in it goes negative. One number per interval cannot separate a smaller dividend from cheaper borrow. You need an outside fact for one of them, and on most names the dividend is the one you can look up. [equation: D_implied = F(T_1) × e^(r − b)(T_2 − T_1) − F(T_2)] Reads as: grow the near forward to the far date at the rate less the borrow fee; whatever the far forward falls short by is the dividend the market expects in between. A roll between two expiries that straddle an ex-date has one unknown, so trading it is trading that dividend and nothing else. Each round below gives you a company, a headline and the dividend the roll implies. Buy the roll if you think the announced dividend will come in above that number, sell it if below, or pass. Fifty contracts: every cent of dividend is $50. Trade the roll into the board meeting Your roll In the first round the market prices an 18% chance that a quiet board suspends a $0.80 dividend, so the roll implies $0.658; the board pays the $0.80 and a bought roll makes $710. Over 2,000 rounds, buying every roll loses about $35 a round and selling every one makes about the same: the market's number is close to fair on average. Trading only where your chance of a cut differs from the market's averages $331 a round. The roll pays for being right about the dividend and for nothing else. Trader's lens Dividend traders read the implied dividend off the options the way bond traders read a yield: the number the market has agreed on, to be compared with their own. The view is a probability of a cut and its size; the roll is the cleanest way to hold that view, because the stock's direction and its volatility cancel out of it. Implied dividends move on the same news as credit: earnings misses, peer cuts, spreads widening. The tail is one-sided. A dividend rarely rises by surprise and often falls to zero. Size from the cut, not the cent: a suspension moves the roll by the whole dividend. Rule of thumb: implied dividend ≈ regular dividend × (1 − market's chance of a cut × size of the cut).

chapters.title: A dividend change is a delta nobody hedged
chapters.dek: Hold the stock price still and change the dividend. The options move anyway, and a conversion moves most of all.

figures.title: P&L per contract when the dividend changes
figures.caption: The call and put lines are always the same distance apart, and that distance is the green line. A conversion's dividend exposure does not depend on the strike.

checks.q: You are long 500 one-year conversions on a stock paying $0.60 a quarter. The company halves the dividend and the stock is unchanged. Roughly what happens?
checks.why: You lose about $58,000. Four dividends fall inside the year, halving them removes $1.17 of present value, and each conversion loses $116: 500 × $116. The loan was locked in on the interest rate and on the strike, and on nothing else. The last answer applies a delta to a position that has none.

chapters.text: The company halves its dividend, 60 cents to 30, and for the purpose of the figure the stock does not react. Every forward rises by the dividends that will no longer be paid. The figure shows what that does to a two-year call, a two-year put and a conversion, per contract, at each strike. P&L per contract when the dividend changes The change The call and put lines are always the same distance apart, and that distance is the green line. A conversion's dividend exposure does not depend on the strike. Eight dividends fall before the two-year expiry, and halving them removes $2.30 of present value. The at-the-money call gains $138 a contract and the put loses $87. The call takes 60% of the change and the put most of the rest, which is roughly the split of their deltas: a higher forward is worth to an option what a higher stock price would be. The conversion loses $225 a contract at every strike. It was long the stock in order to collect those dividends, and it had sold the forward at a price that assumed them. A reversal makes the same $225. This is the sense in which a conversion is long dividends and a reversal is short them: completely, with no delta to dilute it. The assumption that the stock holds still is the generous one. A cut usually comes with a falling share price, and a book of conversions on a company in trouble is long the stock's dividends at the moment they are least safe. That is why the implied dividend in chapter 02 is worth reading before the announcement and not after. [equation: Δ(C − P) = − ΔPV(dividends) × e^−bT] Reads as: call-minus-put at any strike rises by the present value of the dividends removed, shaded slightly for the borrow fee. A conversion is short call-minus-put, so it loses exactly that. Try this Raise the dividend instead. Predict which side of a conversion desk is pleased. Derivation — why the forward is all you need A call minus a put at one strike pays the stock minus the strike at expiry, with certainty. Its value today is therefore the present value of the forward minus the strike. [equation: C − P = e^−rT ( F − K )] Reads as: the synthetic is worth the discounted gap between the forward and the strike. The forward itself is the stock, less the dividends a holder collects before expiry, grown at the interest rate and shrunk by what a lender of the shares is paid. Nothing about volatility enters, which is why these readings survive any argument about the smile. Where it breaks. American options can be exercised early, and the right is worth most exactly around dividends and on hard-to-borrow names, so listed call-minus-put is not a clean forward there; use strikes near the money, where the early-exercise value is smallest, or the roll. Dividends are treated as known cash amounts and the borrow fee as a smooth curve. Real fees jump, real shares get recalled, and a forward that looks rich can be a loan nobody will let you keep.
